data.text/html:
AI lost to a 3-line algorithm: PID vs. neural networks

An interactive companion to Graduate ML's video "AI Lost to A 3 Line Algorithm".
You probably think you need AI to keep a self-balancing robot upright. A controller so simple it fits in three lines (proportional, integral, derivative) does the job. So when do you actually need the neural network?

data.text/markdown:
Google's first rule of ML ("don't be afraid to launch without machine learning") is the thread through this lesson. We follow the video's order:
# Section What you'll touch
1 Calculus in 60 seconds rectangles under a curve, a secant line that shrinks into a tangent
2 PID: the three-part story a live balancing robot with Kp / Ki / Kd knobs
3 Neurons, and why they need a bend stack linear layers until they collapse, then drag a response curve that ReLUs must fit
4 Choosing between AI and PID add a load, climb a hill, face unknown worlds
5 Sandbox, quiz, recap free play and a self-check
Color language (used everywhere): red = error / lean angle θ, orange = P term, purple = I term, teal = D term, blue = neural network / ReLU, grey = the target or a reference.

1 · Calculus in under 60 seconds

The robot's controller uses exactly two ideas from calculus, so we'll start there, as the video does. Integral: stack rectangles. Put rectangles under the curve and add up their areas. Make them thinner, and thinner, infinitely thin, and the sum becomes the area under the curve: ||[\int_0^T e(t)\,dt \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n} e(t_k)\,\Delta t .||]Derivative: squeeze a secant. Take two points, find the slope between them, then push them infinitely close together: ||[\frac{de}{dt}(t_0) \;=\; \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{e(t_0+h)-e(t_0)}{h}.||]The curve below is an error signal ||(e(t)||) (red), how far a robot is from upright over time. Area below zero counts as negative.

data.text/markdown:
2 · PID: a big equation that is a simple three-part story

||[ u(t) \;=\; \underbrace{\color{#f18f01}{K_p\, e(t)}}_{\text{now}} \;+\; \underbrace{\color{#6c5b7b}{K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\,d\tau}}_{\text{memory}} \;+\; \underbrace{\color{#2a9d8f}{K_d\, \frac{de}{dt}}}_{\text{trend}} ||]
  • P reacts to the current error: lean more, push harder.
  • I reacts to the error accumulated over time (the area under the error curve from section 1). It gives the robot memory.
  • D reacts to how quickly the error is changing (the slope from section 1). It makes the robot less jerky.
  • Each K is a gain you tune by hand, using physics or brute force. ||(u(t)||) is how hard the motor drives.
In code, that is three lines: 
integral += e * dt
derivative = (e - e_prev) / dt
u = Kp * e + Ki * integral + Kd * derivative
Our robot is an inverted pendulum on a wheel. The lean angle ||(\theta||) obeys ||(\ddot\theta = \tfrac{g}{L}\sin\theta + \tfrac{u}{m}\cos\theta + d||), where ||(m||) is the load, ||(d||) is a disturbance (a hill), and the error is ||(e=-\theta||) (target: upright). The simulator below runs this physics live in your browser.

data.text/markdown:
3 · Neural networks, and why they need to get "curve-ier"

A neuron takes inputs, multiplies them by weights, adds a bias: ||(y = w\cdot x + b||), which is just ||(y = mx + b||). Stack many neurons into layers and... you'd think you get something powerful. The catch: a weighted sum of weighted sums is still a weighted sum. ||[W_3\big(W_2(W_1x+b_1)+b_2\big)+b_3 \;=\; \underbrace{(W_3W_2W_1)}_{W}\,x + \underbrace{(\dots)}_{b}||]Without an activation function, a deep network is no different from a single layer. Check it yourself below.

ReLU: add one bend

The fix is an activation function that bends each neuron's output. The simplest effective one is ReLU, the rectified linear unit: ||[\operatorname{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z)\qquad\text{negative} \to 0,\quad \text{positive} \to \text{unchanged}.||]One bend is enough. Adding up many shifted, scaled ReLUs, ||(\;\hat u(\theta)=b+\sum_j w_j\,\operatorname{ReLU}(\theta-c_j)\;||), can trace any curve, piece by piece. That matters for the robot. A linear controller that sees twice the lean doubles the motor, always. A real robot may want something else: a gentle response near upright, a hard shove at large angles, saturation at the motor's limit. Drag the blue dots to design the response you'd like ("motor command vs. lean"). Then see who can follow it: a single neuron ||(y=mx+b||), or a ReLU network.

Both models are perfect: if the world is linear, you don't need the bend.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eClick \u003cstrong\u003eDeadzone + shove\u003c/strong\u003e and slide neurons from 1 to 24. Every extra ReLU adds one more corner, and the error collapses.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eClick \u003cstrong\u003eAsymmetric\u003c/strong\u003e: lean forward → push hard, lean back → push gently. The orange line can't do it. That's the video's point\n   about how \"a 10° lean while accelerating backwards doesn't need the same response as a 10° lean standing still\": a \u003cstrong\u003enon-linear\u003c/strong\u003e response.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNote the \u003cstrong\u003ePID\u003c/strong\u003e is a \u003cem\u003esum of linear terms\u003c/em\u003e in the error. Its shape is fixed; only the K's slide it around.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · Choosing between AI and PID

Both robots can balance. So why ever use the one with AI? The video gives three tests, and most people forget the last one.
  1. Add a load. The K's were tuned for the robot's physics. Change the physics (heavier load = sluggish motor response, ||(u/m||)) and the old gains may no longer work.
  2. Climb a hill. A constant push ||(d||) from the slope. Now the I term earns its keep, but the best gains shift again.
  3. Unknown worlds. If you don't know the challenge in advance, you'd have to tune a PID for every imaginable environment. You'd never finish.
Below, the "your PID" line uses the gains you set on the live robot in section 2. The "re-tuned PID" is what you'd get by brute-force searching gains for this exact world, which is the job a learning controller does automatically.

Watch the blue cross on the\n   heatmap slide right, toward a bigger Kp and Kd (≈ 60→110 and 11→25). \u003cem\u003eSame algorithm, new physics, new gains.\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eBack at m = 1, set a \u003cstrong\u003e15° hill\u003c/strong\u003e. Go to section 2, set \u003cstrong\u003eKi = 0\u003c/strong\u003e, and return: the red line now settles \u003cem\u003etilted\u003c/em\u003e (a steady-state error).\n   Only the integral's memory removes it.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eCombine a heavy load with a steep hill. The good region on the heatmap shrinks. That's the \"when the forces change, the gains need to change\" story.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
Test 3: many unknown worlds

Now we don't know the world in advance. We draw random worlds (load 0.5–4×, slope ±15°) and compare three strategies:
  • your PID: one fixed set of gains, deployed everywhere.
  • best single PID: the one gain triple (from our search grid) that does best on average over all worlds. This is careful robust tuning, done by brute force.
  • adapt per world: re-tune for each world. This is an upper bound on what an adaptive/learning controller could achieve.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat to notice\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe fixed PID tuned for one world falls in many heavy-load worlds.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eRobust tuning gets you a long way: one cleverly chosen PID often survives almost everything here. That is the \u003cem\u003elaw of least power\u003c/em\u003e in action.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eBut \"adapt per world\" always has lower cost, because the best gains really do differ between worlds. The more varied and unknown the worlds,\n  the bigger that gap, and the stronger the case for a controller that \u003cstrong\u003elearns\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"success"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
The verdict

PID (3 lines) Neural network
Shape of response sum of linear terms in the error any non-linear function (ReLU bends)
Setup tune 3 gains by hand collect data, train (time!)
Deploy & debug trivial, interpretable complex, harder to trust
Physics change (load, hill) must be re-tuned can adapt
Best for simple, known, stable problems varied, unknown, non-linear problems
Start with the dumb algorithm. Reach for AI when the world refuses to stay simple.

5 · Sandbox: break the robot

Every knob in one place, including two the video hints at: sensor noise (the D term differentiates noise, so it amplifies jitter) and the motor limit (a real motor can't push infinitely hard, which is itself a non-linearity a PID doesn't know about).

Look at the teal D trace: it turns into static. Find the smallest Kd that still balances.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMotor limit:\u003c/strong\u003e set the initial lean to 0.8 rad and the motor limit to 10. No gains can save it: gravity's pull (\u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(19.6\\sin 0.8 ≈ 14||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e) is stronger than the saturated motor. Raise the limit until some gains work.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHill hero:\u003c/strong\u003e with m = 3 and a 12° hill, find gains with cost &lt; 1.0 (hint: you'll need all three terms, and big ones).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
Recap

Idea One-liner Where you touched it
Integral add infinitely thin rectangles → area under the curve §1 rectangle slider
Derivative squeeze a secant → slope at a point §1 gap h slider
P term react to the error now §2 live robot, Kp
I term react to accumulated error (memory); kills steady tilt on hills §2 Ki, §4 hill
D term react to how fast the error changes; less jerky, but amplifies noise §2 Kd, §5 noise
Gains K tuned by physics or brute force; depend on the system §4 heatmap
Linear collapse stacked linear layers = one neuron ||(y=mx+b||) §3 depth slider
ReLU ||(\max(0,z)||); sums of bends fit any curve → non-linear control §3 response designer
PID vs. AI PID: simple, reliable, doesn't adapt. NN: adapts, costs training and complexity §4 unknown worlds
Rule of thumb: launch the 3-line algorithm first, and bring in learning when the world gets too varied to hand-tune.
